conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team. I know you’ve been having severe abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me more about what brought you in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had terrible cramping for two days—no bowel movements, no gas. I couldn’t keep anything down, not even through my tube. It felt worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of gastroparesis and a feeding tube. We did a CT scan, and it showed something serious—your cecum, part of your colon, has twisted. That’s called a cecal volvulus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Twisted? Is that why I couldn’t pass anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The twist is blocking your bowel. Worse, the blood supply is compromised—there’s early signs of ischemia. This needs surgery, and soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? Again? I’ve had so many… What kind of surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do an exploratory laparotomy. We’ll remove the twisted part of your colon—the right side—and reconnect your intestine. There’s also something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT suggests the wires from your old gastric pacemaker may have caused the twist. They’re looping into your bowel. We’ll remove the device and wires during the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I forgot I even had that pacemaker. Is it dangerous to remove?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s safe, and necessary. Leaving it could cause more problems. We’ve discussed this with your family, and we have your consent. We’ll prepare you for the OR now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through surgery. You had a right hemicolectomy and the pacemaker with its wires was removed. The anastomosis looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I feel? I’m so groggy… Was everything okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgery went well—no complications. You’re on a PCA pump for pain. You have an NG tube for now, and we’re giving fluids and antibiotics through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to wait for your bowel to wake up. We’ll start tube feeds once we hear bowel sounds and you pass gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your NG tube is out. You’re passing gas, and your belly is less distended. We’ll keep you NPO for now, but we’re close to starting feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My throat was so sore from the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count was high but is coming down. That means the infection risk is improving. We’re still holding off on feeds—just a little longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start your tube feeds today—slowly, at half goal. We’ll monitor for nausea or bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m still feeling a bit nauseous. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially after surgery and with your history. We’ll give you anti-nausea meds and go slow. If you tolerate this, we’ll increase tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well with the feeds. We’re increasing to full rate. Your labs are stable, and you’re walking more each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today, we’re exchanging your GJ tube to one with separate G and J ports. It’ll give us more flexibility with feeding and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a big procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s done endoscopically with light sedation. You’ll be back soon, and we’ll restart feeds through the new tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube exchange went smoothly. You’re back on full feeds. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit sore at the site, but okay. Still nauseous when I try to eat by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expected that. We’re going to try clamping your tube for short periods to see if you can tolerate oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve always had trouble keeping food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we need to assess if it’s mechanical or motility-related. We’ll schedule a gastric emptying study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gastric emptying study came back normal. Liquids are leaving your stomach at a normal rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why do I feel so full and nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an upper GI study too. It shows your Nissen fundoplication is intact, no narrowing. But there’s moderate esophageal dysmotility—your esophagus isn’t moving food down well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my stomach, it’s my esophagus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That explains the nausea when you try to eat. We’ll adjust your diet and add a new anti-nausea med. You’ll follow up with GI after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating clamping trials better. We’re advancing your diet to regular food in small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a few bites yesterday and didn’t vomit. That’s progress!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your incision is healing well—no redness or drainage. Pain is controlled with oral meds now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’re walking independently, tolerating a regular diet, and your feeds are at goal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your labs are stable, vitals are good. Home health will help with your GJ tube and feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue levothyroxine, citalopram, omeprazole. We’re adding dronabinol and trimethobenzamide for nausea, as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your surgeon in two weeks. GI will evaluate your esophageal dysmotility. Call us if you have fever, vomiting, or incision problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about lifting or driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lifting over five pounds for four weeks. Don’t drive while on pain meds. Showering is okay—just keep the incision dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the steri-strips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll fall off on their own. Remove any left after ten days. Staples will be removed at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about managing the tube at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Home health will train you and your caregiver. They’ll visit several times a week at first. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel more confident now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep resting, stay hydrated, and keep walking. You’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, you’re tolerating everything well. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t wait to be home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be here if you need us. Take care, and see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I get the flu shot this year?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. It’s especially important with your medical history. Your primary care can give it in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’ll schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Rest well, and don’t hesitate to call with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned that the hard way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re doing great. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and meds shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Call us if anything’s unclear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for being so thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s our job. You’ve been a great patient—cooperative and strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been a lot, but I’m glad it’s over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you came through it well. Recovery will take time, but you’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll miss you, but we’re glad you’re going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll miss you all too. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been our privilege. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.
